title: Teenager with knee pain after football

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi, Ethan. Hi, come in. And you're Mum?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What can I do for you, Ethan?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My knee's been hurting. Just below the kneecap.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long has it been sore?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not really. It just started hurting after football.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How much football do you play?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Training three times a week, and a match on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: During and after football. And kneeling on it really hurts.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Does it ever wake you up at night?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Is it sore when you're resting?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any swelling of the knee, or does it lock or give way?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any pain in your hip or your thigh?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any fevers, or losing weight, or feeling unwell?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: His brother had exactly this when he was fourteen. It was Osgood-something.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's useful to know. Has Ethan had any problems with his joints before?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, can you lie on the couch for me? I'm going to feel around your knee. There's a tender bony lump just below the kneecap, on the right shin bone. That's called the tibial tuberosity.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: There's no fluid in the knee. You can bend and straighten it fully. The ligaments feel stable. Let me check your hips. I'm moving your right hip around, and the left. Any pain?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Both hips have a full range of movement with no pain. Can you walk to the door and back? That's a normal walk.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: This is Osgood-Schlatter disease, like your brother had. It's an irritation where the tendon from your kneecap attaches to your shin bone. It's very common in active teenagers having a growth spurt, and it settles as you finish growing.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do I have to stop football?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Not completely. Cut down for a few weeks. Let the pain guide you. If it hurts a lot during or after, do less.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Ice it for 15 minutes after sport. For pain you can take paracetamol, or ibuprofen 400 milligrams up to three times a day with food.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll refer you to physiotherapy for some stretching exercises for your thigh muscles.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If it hasn't settled in six to eight weeks, come back. But come back sooner if the pain wakes you at night, the knee swells up, you get a fever, start limping all the time, or get pain in your hip.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Pain below the right kneecap for 2 months.
reference_note.history: Gradual onset without specific injury; plays football (training three times a week plus matches) and school PE. Pain during and after sport and on kneeling. No night pain. No rest pain. No swelling, locking or giving way. No hip or thigh pain. No fever or weight loss. Limps only after matches. Older brother had Osgood-Schlatter disease at a similar age. No previous joint problems.
reference_note.medications_allergies: No regular medications. No known drug allergies. No asthma or peptic ulcer disease.
reference_note.examination: Tender bony prominence over the right tibial tuberosity. No knee effusion. Full range of knee movement; ligaments stable. Both hips: full, pain-free range of movement. Normal gait.
reference_note.impression: Osgood-Schlatter disease of the right knee. No red flags.
reference_note.plan: Activity modification guided by pain. Ice for 15 minutes after sport. Paracetamol or ibuprofen 400 mg up to three times daily with food as needed. Refer to physiotherapy for quadriceps and hamstring stretching. Review if not settling in 6–8 weeks.
reference_note.safety_netting: Return sooner if night pain, knee swelling, fever, persistent limp or hip pain.
